Issued at 445 AM EDT FRI JUL 31 2026

The first part of the extended will be dealing with a seemingly
too early synoptic low slowly working east through the eastern
Ohio Valley. This will keep low clouds and some, mostly 
stratiform, rain around well into the start of the new work week 
- eventually taking on a diurnal pattern to the convection.

The previous long term discussion follows:

The long-term period opens 12Z Saturday with a positively-tilted 
500 hPa shortwave trough digging into the Mid-Mississippi Valley 
behind shortwave ridging departing east of the Appalachians. An 
~1003 mb area of low pressure will be situated over southwest 
Illinois just ahead of the shortwave trough. A warm front will
extend southeast from the low across Middle Tennessee and Northern
Georgia, while a cold front arcs to the south into the Missouri 
Bootheel and then southwest to over Northern Texas. Further to the 
north, 500 hPa troughing is focused over and adjacent to Hudson and 
James Bay, supporting a second cold front draped from a surface low 
over southern Baffin Island southward to the Ottawa Valley, and then 
westward across the Upper Great Lakes and Dakotas. Meanwhile further
west, an ~599 dam high is situated over the Lower Colorado River 
basin while a ridge axis extends northeastward across the Canadian 
Prairie Provinces.

The most active weather of the long-term forecast will occur during 
the first two days of the period. The aforementioned shortwave
trough will continue to amplify as it becomes more meridionally 
oriented on Saturday and Saturday night while its attendant surface 
low tracks over the Lower Ohio Valley. This will send the warm front 
pushing into eastern Kentucky while the trailing cold front catches 
up and occludes. At the same time, the northerly trough will also 
amplify across the Great Lakes and capture some or much of the 
vorticity energy associated with the more southerly shortwave. There 
is admittedly substantial disparity from model- to-model and run- 
to-run regarding how much upper-level support remains with the 
closed-off low or perturbation that lingers. In any case, the much 
diminished upper-level support of the surface low leaves it to
meander southward and dissipate early next week along with its 
associated frontal structures as relatively subtle weakness lingers 
in the heights aloft. Meanwhile, a new area of low pressure will
form near or over the Eastern Great Lakes and New England as the 
northern stream trough pulls away to the east. The system's cold 
front will sag southward into the Central Appalachians through mid- 
week but stagnate there. Another upper level trough and cold front 
may approach the Ohio Valley around and just beyond the end of the 
forecast period.

The main concern during the long-term period will be the potential
for heavy rainfall on Saturday into early Sunday as PWATs rise to
1.75 to 2.00 inches (or 90th to 95th percentile relative to climo)
in the WAA regime ahead of the surface low. WPC's Slight Risk (2
of 4) for excessive rainfall was expanded to cover all but the 
easternmost portions of Pike County. Efficient warm layer rainfall
processes combined with the potential for training convection in 
a high PWAT environment are all supportive of a locally heavy 
rainfall threat, possibly leading to instances of flooding. A 
notable mitigating factor is the antecedent drying ongoing prior 
to the event---the 3-hour FFG currently ranges from 1.75 to 2.50 
inches across most of the JKL CWA and will likely improve further 
with an additional 36 to 48 hours of drying. As for any severe 
weather potential, shear may be sufficient for limited organization, 
but overall destabilization remains highly uncertain, especially 
east of I-75. If any strong to severe storms materialize, they would
most likely occur west of I-75. PWATs fall back somewhat Sunday and
Sunday night as the surface low weakens and dissipates, but the 
second cold front fails to press far enough south to drop PWAT 
levels below seasonal norms. Lingering moisture combined with the 
remnant weakness aloft will still combine with the daily heating 
cycle to keep the continued threat for primarily afternoon and 
evening convection in the forecast from Monday onward.

In sensible weather terms, clouds and shower and thunderstorm
chances increase on Saturday, with coverage peaking Saturday 
night followed by a secondary peak on Sunday afternoon. Some of 
the showers and thunderstorms could produce torrential downpours, 
especially on Saturday and Saturday night. It will be muggy both 
weekend days with high temperatures mainly in the lower 80s and 
lows not far from 70F. Looking ahead to the new work week, 
temperatures start the week with highs near 80F on Monday before 
slowly warming into the mid to upper 80s by Thursday, while 
nighttime lows range from the 60s to near 70F. Scattered showers
